sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we de grammatica van #dutchgrammar 2 les 20 over modale werkwoorden in combinatie met het woordje van.
sentences.en: Today we practise the grammar of #dutchgrammar 2 lesson 20, about modal verbs combined with the little word van.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Vandaag (Today) oefenen (practice) we (we) de grammatica (the grammar) van (of) #dutchgrammar 2 (#dutchgrammar 2) les 20 (lesson 20) over (about) modale werkwoorden (modal verbs) in combinatie met (in combination with) het woordje (the little word) van (van / of).  
• Natural translation: Today we are practicing the grammar from #dutchgrammar 2, lesson 20, about modal verbs in combination with the word "van".

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subject-Verb Inversion (V2 Rule):** Because the sentence starts with a time element (*Vandaag*), the verb (*oefenen*) must stay in the second position, forcing the subject (*we*) to move after the verb.  
• **Diminutive (*-je*):** *Het woordje* is the diminutive of *het woord* (the word). Dutch speakers frequently use diminutives to refer to specific, short words or particles in a casual, friendly way.  
• **Fixed Prepositional Phrase:** *In combinatie met* is a standard, useful chunk meaning "in combination with" or "combined with."  

• **Extensions:**  
– Morgen bespreken we hoofdstuk drie over voornaamwoorden. (Tomorrow we are discussing chapter three about pronouns.)  
– Dit medicijn is gevaarlijk in combinatie met alcohol. (This medication is dangerous in combination with alcohol.)  
– Wat betekent het woordje 'er' in deze zin? (What does the little word 'er' mean in this sentence?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vanavond herhalen we de woordenlijst van hoofdstuk vier over reizen in combinatie met het openbaar vervoer. (Tonight we are reviewing the vocabulary list from chapter four about traveling in combination with public transport.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "#dutchgrammar" refers to a very popular series of Dutch language learning courses and textbooks created by Bart de Pau (Learndutch.org), a staple resource in the international expat and student community in the Netherlands.  
• The grammar topic mentioned (modal verbs + *van*) refers to a very typical colloquial Dutch structure used to quote attitudes or habits, such as *"Ik moet van mijn moeder mijn kamer opruimen"* (My mom says I have to clean my room — literally: "I must from my mother clean my room").

sentences.nl: Xing, Annika en Marieke hebben een beetje ruzie.
sentences.en: Xing, Annika and Marieke are having a bit of a fight.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Xing, Annika en Marieke** = Xing, Annika and Marieke  
• **hebben** = have  
• **een beetje** = a little bit  
• **ruzie** = quarrel / argument  

*(Natural translation: Xing, Annika, and Marieke are having a bit of an argument.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Idiom ("ruzie hebben"):** In English, you *have an* argument, or you *are* arguing. In Dutch, the standard expression is *ruzie hebben* (literally: to have quarrel), without an article like *een* directly before the noun.  
• **Quantifier ("een beetje"):** *Een beetje* means "a little bit." It is inserted directly before the uncountable noun *ruzie* to soften the statement, modifying it to mean a minor disagreement rather than a big fight.  
• **Plural Verb Agreement:** Because the subject consists of three people (*Xing, Annika en Marieke*), it is plural ("they"), so the verb *hebben* (to have) takes the plural form.

**Extensions:**  
• Wij hebben nooit ruzie. (We never argue / We never have fights.)  
• Ik heb een beetje honger. (I am a little bit hungry — *literally: I have a bit hunger.*)  
• Hebben jullie alweer ruzie? (Are you guys arguing again?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De broers hebben een beetje ruzie over het nieuwe speelgoed. (The brothers are having a bit of an argument about the new toy.)

sentences.nl: Xing heeft verteld dat Martin een vriendin heeft.
sentences.en: Xing has told them that Martin has a girlfriend.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing (Xing) heeft (has) verteld (told) dat (that) Martin (Martin) een (a) vriendin (girlfriend / female friend) heeft (has).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Present Perfect (Voltooid Tegenwoordige Tijd):** The main clause uses the auxiliary verb *heeft* (from *hebben*) + the past participle *verteld* (from *vertellen* - to tell). Verbs starting with the unstressed prefix *ver-* do not get the *ge-* prefix in the past participle.  
• **Subordinate Clause (Bijzin) Word Order:** The conjunction *dat* (that) introduces a subordinate clause. In Dutch, *dat* pushes all verbs in that clause to the very end of the sentence (*...dat Martin een vriendin **heeft***).  
• **Extensions:**  
– Zij heeft gezegd dat hij morgen komt. (She has said that he is coming tomorrow.)  
– Ik heb gehoord dat jij een nieuwe baan hebt. (I have heard that you have a new job.)  
– Heb je verteld dat we gaan verhuizen? (Have you told [them] that we are going to move?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Anna heeft verteld dat haar broer een nieuwe auto heeft. (Anna told us that her brother has a new car.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Vriendin vs. een vriendin:** In Dutch, *vriendin* means both "female friend" and "girlfriend." Saying someone has *een vriendin* (a girlfriend) without further context almost always implies a romantic partner. To specify a platonic female friend, Dutch people usually say *een vriendin van hem* (a friend of his) or *een gewone vriendin* (a regular female friend).

sentences.nl: Xing heeft niet gezegd dat zij dat is, want dat mag ze niet van Martin.
sentences.en: Xing hasn't said that it's her, because Martin doesn't allow her to.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing (Xing) heeft (has) niet (not) gezegd (said) dat (that) zij (she) dat (that) is (is), want (because) dat (that) mag (may / is allowed to) ze (she) niet (not) van (from/by) Martin (Martin).  
• Natural translation: "Xing didn't say that that's her, because Martin won't let her."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subordinate clause word order:** The word *dat* (that) introduces a subordinate clause, which pushes the conjugated verb *is* to the very end of that clause (*...dat zij dat is*).  
• **Coordinating conjunction:** The word *want* (because) connects two main clauses and does **not** send the verb to the end. Notice the inversion in the second clause: because it starts with the object *dat* for emphasis, the verb *mag* comes before the subject *ze* (*...want dat mag ze niet*).  
• **Idiom "mogen van":** In Dutch, to express that someone allows or forbids you to do something, you use the verb *mogen* (to be allowed to) + the preposition *van* (from) + [Person]. The main action verb (here, "to say") is often left out because it is implied.  
• **Zij vs. Ze:** Both mean "she." *Zij* is the stressed form (used here to emphasize that *she* is the person in question), while *ze* is the unstressed form used in the second half.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik mag niet gaan van mijn moeder. (My mother won't let me go / I am not allowed to go by my mother.)  
• Hij heeft niet verteld dat hij ziek is. (He didn't tell [us] that he is sick.)  
• Dat moet ik van mijn baas. (My boss is making me do that / I have to do that because of my boss.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Lisa heeft niet verteld dat zij de winnaar is, want dat mag ze niet van de jury. (Lisa didn't tell anyone that she is the winner, because the jury won't let her.)

sentences.nl: Dat hebben ze afgesproken.
sentences.en: They agreed on that.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Dat** (That) **hebben** (have) **ze** (they) **afgesproken** (agreed-upon / arranged).  
• Natural translation: "They agreed on that." or "That's what they arranged."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Topicalization & Inversion:** The object (**Dat**) is placed at the very beginning of the sentence to emphasize it. Because Dutch requires the conjugated verb to stay in the second position (V2 rule), the subject (**ze**) and the verb (**hebben**) swap places. (Standard order: *Ze hebben dat afgesproken*).  
• **Separable Verb in Present Perfect:** *Afspreken* (to agree/arrange/meet up) is a separable verb (*af* + *spreken*). In the present perfect tense, the *ge-* prefix goes right between the prefix and the main verb stem: **af** + **ge** + **sproken**.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Dat hebben we gisteren besloten.* (We decided that yesterday.)  
  – *Hoe laat hebben jullie afgesproken?* (What time did you guys agree to meet?)  
  – *Dat heb ik niet gezegd.* (I didn't say that.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dat hebben we vorige week al geregeld. (We already arranged that last week.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Afspreken* is a cornerstone of Dutch agenda culture. The Dutch are famous for planning social engagements weeks in advance. Once something is *afgesproken*, it is treated as a firm commitment. Saying *"Dat hebben we afgesproken"* is a very common, direct way in both business and personal life to remind someone that a deal is a deal.

sentences.nl: Marieke is natuurlijk verdrietig.
sentences.en: Marieke is sad, of course.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke (Marieke) is (is) natuurlijk (naturally / of course) verdrietig (sad).

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb Second (V2):** As a standard Dutch declarative sentence, the conjugated verb *is* (from *zijn*, to be) is in the second position, immediately following the subject *Marieke*.
• **Adverb Placement:** The sentence adverb *natuurlijk* (of course / naturally) is placed after the conjugated verb and right before the predicate adjective *verdrietig* to modify the entire statement.
• **Predicate Adjective:** Because *verdrietig* does not come directly before a noun, it remains in its base form without an *-e* ending.
• **Extensions:**
  – Hij is natuurlijk moe. (He is of course tired.)
  – Wij zijn een beetje verdrietig. (We are a little bit sad.)
  – Dat is natuurlijk waar. (That is naturally true.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De kinderen zijn natuurlijk erg blij met het cadeau. (The children are of course very happy with the gift.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Natuurlijk* (often shortened to *tuurlijk* in spoken Dutch) is one of the most common filler and confirmation words in the Netherlands. The Dutch use it constantly to show empathy or agreement in conversation, similar to saying "of course" or "obviously" in English.

sentences.nl: Zij vindt Martin leuk en ze wilde met hem romantisch naar de maan kijken.
sentences.en: She likes Martin and she wanted to look at the moon with him, romantically.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Zij (She) vindt (finds) Martin (Martin) leuk (nice/likeable) en (and) ze (she) wilde (wanted) met (with) hem (him) romantisch (romantically) naar (at/to) de (the) maan (moon) kijken (to look).  
• Natural translation: She likes Martin and she wanted to romantically look at the moon with him.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **[Iemand] leuk vinden**: In Dutch, to express that you "like" someone (platonically or romantically), you literally say you "find someone nice" (*iemand leuk vinden*). Note how *Martin* is placed between the verb *vindt* and the adjective *leuk*.  
• **Zij vs. Ze**: Both mean "she." *Zij* is the stressed form (used here at the start to emphasize **she** is the one who likes him), while *ze* is the unstressed, more casual form used in the second half of the sentence so it doesn't sound repetitive.  
• **Modal verb word order**: In the second clause, *wilde* (past tense of *willen* - to want) is the conjugated modal verb in the second position. Because of this, the main action verb *kijken* (to look) is pushed all the way to the end of the sentence in its infinitive form.  
• **Kijken naar**: Just as English uses the preposition "at" with "look", Dutch pairs the verb *kijken* with the preposition *naar* (literally "to/towards").

**Extensions:**  
• Ik vind haar erg leuk. (I really like her.)  
• Hij wilde gisteren naar een film kijken. (He wanted to watch a movie yesterday.)  
• Wij kijken samen naar de sterren. (We are looking at the stars together.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij vindt haar leuk en hij wilde met haar gezellig naar de zonsondergang kijken.  
(He likes her and he wanted to cozily look at the sunset with her.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch dating culture, saying *ik vind je leuk* is the standard way to confess romantic interest early on. Moving up to *ik hou van je* (I love you) is considered a very big, serious step and is saved for much later in an established relationship.

sentences.nl: Annika is een beetje boos op Xing.
sentences.en: Annika is a bit angry with Xing.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Annika = Annika  
• is = is  
• een beetje = a little bit  
• boos = angry / mad  
• op = on (here: at / with)  
• Xing = Xing  
• **Natural translation:** Annika is a little bit angry at Xing.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Boos op:** In Dutch, the fixed preposition used with *boos* (angry) is **op** (literally "on") when referring to a person, whereas English uses "at" or "with."  
• **Een beetje:** Literally meaning "a little bite," this is a very common adverbial phrase used to soften adjectives or verbs, functioning just like "a bit" or "a little" in English.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik ben **een beetje** moe vandaag. (I am a little bit tired today.)  
– Waarom ben je **boos op** mij? (Why are you mad at me?)  
– Hij is **een beetje** verliefd **op** haar. (He is a little bit in love with her. — *Note: "verliefd" also takes the preposition "op".*)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De leraar is een beetje boos op de studenten omdat ze te laat zijn. (The teacher is a little bit angry with the students because they are late.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Dutch are famous for using diminutives (words ending in *-je*, *-tje*, *-pje*) not just to indicate small physical size, but also to soften the emotional impact of a statement. Adding **een beetje** (a little bit) is a classic way for Dutch speakers to make criticism or negative emotions (like being *boos*) sound less harsh and more manageable in daily conversation.

sentences.nl: Ze mag niet liegen van haar.
sentences.en: Annika won't let her lie.
sentences.note: Spoken order: van haar at the end.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze – She  
• mag – may / is allowed to  
• niet – not  
• liegen – to lie  
• van – from (in this context: by)  
• haar – her  
• (Natural translation: Annika won't let her lie. — haar = Annika, the one who decides.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Mogen + van (Permission from someone):** In Dutch, the modal verb *mogen* (to be allowed to) is combined with the preposition *van* to indicate **who** is granting or denying the permission. English usually uses "by" or rephrases the sentence entirely ("She doesn't let her...").  
• **Sentence structure:** Usually, the *van + [person]* phrase comes before the final infinitive verb (e.g., *Ze mag van haar niet liegen*), though placing it at the very end (*...liegen van haar*) is very common in spoken Dutch as an afterthought or for emphasis.  
• **Extensions:**  
– Ik mag van mijn moeder niet roken. (My mother doesn't allow me to smoke.)  
– Mag jij dat van je baas doen? (Does your boss allow you to do that?)  
– We mogen blijven slapen van oma. (Grandma says we are allowed to sleep over.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij mag van de dokter nog niet werken. (The doctor doesn't allow him to work yet.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch parenting and school culture, the phrasing *"Dat mag niet van..."* (That is not allowed by...) is one of the most common ways children explain rules to each other. You will frequently hear Dutch kids on the playground say, *"Dat mag niet van mijn mama!"* (My mom says I'm not allowed to do that!).

sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ze** (She) **zei** (said) **dat** (that) **het** (it) **bewolkt** (cloudy) **was** (was), **maar** (but) **dat** (that) **was** (was) **niet** (not) **zo** (so/the case).  
• Natural translation: "She said it was cloudy, but it wasn't."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subordinate clause word order:** The conjunction *dat* (that) introduces a subordinate clause, which pushes the conjugated verb (*was*) to the very end of that clause (*...dat het bewolkt was*).  
• **Main clause word order:** The conjunction *maar* (but) is a coordinating conjunction, so the clause following it keeps standard main clause word order, with the verb in the second position (*...maar dat was niet zo*).  
• **Idiom ("Dat is niet zo"):** Literally "That is not so," this is the most natural Dutch way to say "That's not true," "That's not the case," or "It wasn't."  
• **Irregular Past Tense:** *Zei* is the singular simple past tense of *zeggen* (to say). *Was* is the singular simple past of *zijn* (to be).  

**Extensions:**  
• Hij dacht dat het koud was. (He thought that it was cold.)  
• Ik hoop dat het morgen zonnig is. (I hope that it is sunny tomorrow.)  
• Je denkt dat ik boos ben, maar dat is niet zo. (You think that I am angry, but that's not the case.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij zei dat de winkel open was, maar dat was niet zo. (He said that the store was open, but it wasn't.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Talking about the weather is a national pastime in the Netherlands due to its unpredictable marine climate. Because the weather changes so rapidly, someone might genuinely see a cloudy sky (*bewolkt*), only for it to clear up ten minutes later, making sentences like this very common in daily Dutch small talk.

sentences.nl: En Xing zei dat ze niet wist waar Martin was, maar Martin zei dat hij Xing wel heeft gesproken.
sentences.en: And Xing said she didn't know where Martin was, but Martin said he did talk to Xing.
sentences.note: Captions lost zei dat ze niet wist waar; confirmed by speech recognition on the audio.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **En Xing zei** – And Xing said  
• **dat ze niet wist** – that she not knew  
• **waar Martin was,** – where Martin was,  
• **maar Martin zei** – but Martin said  
• **dat hij Xing wel** – that he Xing [indeed/contrary to what was said]  
• **heeft gesproken.** – has spoken.  

*Natural English: And Xing said that she didn't know where Martin was, but Martin said that he actually did speak to Xing.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Subordinate Clauses (*Bijzinnen*):** Words like *dat* (that) and *waar* (where) push the conjugated verbs to the end of their respective clauses (*...dat ze niet **wist*** / *...waar Martin **was*** / *...dat hij Xing wel **heeft gesproken***).  
• **The particle "wel":** *Wel* is the direct opposite of *niet* (not). It has no single English word equivalent, as we usually just stress the auxiliary verb in English (e.g., "he *did* speak to her"). It is used here to contradict Xing's statement.  
• **Spoken Past Tense:** Notice the shift from simple past (*zei, wist, was*) to the present perfect (*heeft gesproken*). In Dutch, the present perfect is heavily favored in spoken language to describe completed past actions, even within reported speech.  
• **Spreken:** You can say *iemand spreken* (to speak to someone) directly without a preposition, though *met iemand spreken* is also correct.  

**Extensions:**  
• Hij denkt **dat** ik het **niet** weet, maar ik weet het **wel**. (He thinks that I don't know it, but I *do* know it.)  
• Ik wist niet **waar** hij **was**. (I did not know where he was.)  
• Heb je de nieuwe manager al **gesproken**? (Have you spoken to the new manager yet?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Anna zei dat ze het boek niet had gezien, maar haar broer zei dat ze het gisteren wel heeft gelezen. (Anna said that she hadn't seen the book, but her brother said that she actually did read it yesterday.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Mastering the word **wel** is a shortcut to sounding truly Dutch. Because Dutch communication values directness and clarity, *wel* is used constantly in daily life to explicitly mark contrast, confirm something positive after a negative assumption, or gently push back in an argument.

sentences.nl: Xing is naar haar kamer gegaan.
sentences.en: Xing has gone to her room.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Xing** – Xing  
• **is** – is (has)  
• **naar** – to  
• **haar** – her  
• **kamer** – room  
• **gegaan** – gone  

• *Natural English:* Xing went to her room. / Xing has gone to her room.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Present Perfect with *Zijn*:** In Dutch, the present perfect tense (*voltooide tijd*) usually uses the auxiliary verb *hebben* (to have). However, verbs that indicate a **change of location or state**—like *gaan* (to go)—use **zijn** (to be) instead. Thus, "is... gegaan" translates to "has gone" or "went".  
• **Sentence Bracket (Tangconstructie):** The auxiliary verb (*is*) stays in the second position, while the past participle (*gegaan*) is sent to the very end of the sentence, wrapping around the rest of the information (*naar haar kamer*).  
• **Preposition *Naar*:** This is the standard preposition used for movement toward a specific direction, place, or person.  

• **Extensions:**  
– Ik **ben naar** de supermarkt **gegaan**. (I went to the supermarket.)  
– Wij **zijn** gisteren **naar** het strand **gegaan**. (We went to the beach yesterday.)  
– **Is** hij al **naar** zijn werk **gegaan**? (Has he gone to his work already?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De kinderen zijn na het avondeten direct naar hun kamer gegaan. (The children went straight to their room after dinner.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch student housing (*studentenhuizen*), renting a room is extremely common and is referred to as *op kamers gaan* (literally: "going on rooms"). Also, in everyday family life, if someone goes to their room (*naar zijn/haar kamer gaan*), it usually implies their bedroom, as the living room is specifically called the *woonkamer* or *huiskamer*.

sentences.nl: Ze moest van Martin haar koffer pakken.
sentences.en: Martin made her pack her suitcase.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze (She) moest (had to) van (from) Martin (Martin) haar (her) koffer (suitcase) pakken (to pack).  
• Natural translation: Martin made her pack her suitcase. / She had to pack her suitcase on Martin's orders.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Idiomatic structure (*moeten van + person*):** In Dutch, to say that someone is making or forcing someone else to do something, you use the verb *moeten* (must/have to) combined with the preposition *van* (from) + the person giving the order. (The opposite, being allowed by someone, uses *mogen van*).  
• **Word Order (Sentence Bracket):** Because there is a modal verb (*moest*, the past tense of *moeten*) in the second position, the main action verb goes to the very end of the sentence as an infinitive (*pakken*).  
• **Vocabulary Note:** *Je koffer pakken* = to pack your suitcase, literally (here: to leave). Not the same as the idiom *je biezen pakken* = to clear off / leave in a hurry.

**Extensions:**  
• Ik moet van mijn moeder mijn kamer opruimen. (My mom is making me clean my room.)  
• Hij mocht van de baas eerder naar huis gaan. (The boss let him go home early.)  
• Wij moeten onze koffers pakken voor de vakantie. (We have to pack our suitcases for the vacation.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij moest van zijn vrouw de auto wassen. (His wife made him wash the car.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None.

sentences.nl: En Martin is buiten.
sentences.en: And Martin is outside.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• En = And  
• Martin = Martin  
• is = is  
• buiten = outside  
• Natural translation: And Martin is outside.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Word Order with "En":** Coordinating conjunctions like *en* (and), *maar* (but), and *want* (because) are "position zero" words. They do not change the normal word order of the sentence that follows. Therefore, the subject (*Martin*) still comes right before the verb (*is*).  
• **Verb "Zijn" (to be):** *Is* is the third-person singular form (he/she/it) of the irregular verb *zijn*.  
• **Adverbs of Place:** *Buiten* means "outside" (the opposite is *binnen*, "inside"). When used with the verb *zijn*, you do not need a preposition like "in" or "at".  
• **Extensions:**  
  – En de hond is binnen. (And the dog is inside.)  
  – Maar Sarah is boven. (But Sarah is upstairs.)  
  – De kinderen zijn buiten. (The children are outside.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik ben binnen, en de kat is buiten. (I am inside, and the cat is outside.)

sentences.nl: Hij heeft Gianluca beloofd te vertellen waar Marieke is.
sentences.en: He promised Gianluca he would tell him where Marieke is.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hij (He) heeft (has) Gianluca (Gianluca) beloofd (promised) te (to) vertellen (tell) waar (where) Marieke (Marieke) is (is).  
• *Natural translation:* He promised Gianluca to tell him where Marieke is.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Present Perfect Tense (Voltooid Tegenwoordige Tijd):** The sentence uses the auxiliary verb *heeft* (has) + the past participle *beloofd* (promised). Note that verbs starting with the prefix *be-* (like *beloven*) do not get the *ge-* prefix in their past participle form.  
• **Infinitive Clause with *te*:** The verb *beloven* (to promise) connects to the next action using *te* + infinitive (*te vertellen* - to tell). Sometimes *om* is added before *te* (*om te vertellen*), which is also correct and very common in spoken Dutch.  
• **Subordinate Clause Word Order (Bijzin):** The word *waar* (where) introduces an indirect question/subordinate clause. In a Dutch subordinate clause, the conjugated verb (*is*) is kicked to the very end of the clause (*...waar Marieke is*).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Zij heeft mij beloofd te helpen. (She promised me to help.)  
  – Kun je me vertellen waar het station is? (Can you tell me where the station is?)  
  – Ik heb hem gevraagd te wachten tot ik klaar ben. (I asked him to wait until I am ready.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij heeft haar moeder beloofd te bellen zodra ze thuis is. (She promised her mother to call as soon as she is home.)

sentences.nl: Gianluca, Marieke is in huisje 65.
sentences.en: Gianluca, Marieke is in cottage 65.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Gianluca, = Gianluca,  
• Marieke = Marieke  
• is = is  
• in = in  
• huisje = little house (cabin/bungalow)  
• 65. = 65 (vijfenzestig).  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Diminutive (-je):** *Huisje* comes from *huis* (house) + the diminutive suffix *-je*. While it literally means "little house," in this context it specifically refers to a vacation bungalow, cabin, or cottage.  
• **Direct Address (Vocative):** Addressing "Gianluca" at the start, separated by a comma, does not affect the word order of the main clause. The sentence still follows the standard Subject-Verb-Rest order (*Marieke is...*).  
• **Number Reading:** In Dutch, two-digit numbers are read with the ones digit before the tens digit, linked by *en* (and). So 65 is read as *vijf-en-zestig* (five-and-sixty).  

**Extensions:**  
• Wij zitten in huisje twaalf. (We are staying in cabin twelve.)  
• Emma, je sleutel ligt in het huisje. (Emma, your key is lying in the cottage.)  
• Mijn tas is in kamer 42. (My bag is in room 42.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Thomas, de familie wacht bij huisje 14. (Thomas, the family is waiting by cabin 14.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Vakantieparken (Holiday Parks):** Renting a *huisje* at a holiday park (like Center Parcs or Landal GreenParks) is a quintessential Dutch vacation tradition. Because these parks often have hundreds of identical or semi-identical bungalows nestled in nature, they are always navigated and referred to simply by their *huisje* number rather than a street address.

sentences.nl: Je mag van mij naar binnen.
sentences.en: You can go in, as far as I'm concerned.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Je (You) mag (may / are allowed to) van mij (from me / as far as I'm concerned) naar binnen (to inside / go in).  
• Natural translation: "You may go inside, as far as I'm concerned." / "I allow you to go inside."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Implied Motion Verb:** In Dutch, when using modal verbs like *mogen* (may) or *moeten* (must) combined with a clear direction like *naar binnen* (inside), the main verb of motion (*gaan* - to go) is usually dropped because it is obvious from context.  
• **Mogen van + [person]:** The structure *mogen van [iemand]* is a very common idiom used to express who is granting the permission. Literally "to be allowed from someone," it translates naturally to "Someone lets me..." or "As far as someone is concerned, I may..."  

• **Extensions:**  
– Je mag van mij nu naar huis. (You can go home now, as far as I'm concerned.)  
– Hij mag van zijn moeder niet naar buiten. (His mother doesn't allow him to go outside.)  
– Kom maar snel naar binnen! (Just come inside quickly!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Je mag van de dokter weer naar buiten. (The doctor says you are allowed to go outside again.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using *van mij* in a sentence with *mogen* is a characteristically direct yet casual Dutch way of giving permission or stating boundaries. Depending on the tone of voice, *Je mag van mij...* can range from warm and welcoming ("Go right ahead!") to slightly indifferent ("I don't mind if you do").

sentences.nl: Dankjewel, Martin.
sentences.en: Thank you, Martin.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Dankjewel = Thank-you-well (Thank you very much)  
• Martin = Martin  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Compound Idiom**: "Dankjewel" (also written as three separate words: *dank je wel*) is a contracted form of *[ik] dank je wel* ("I thank you well").   
• **Informal "Je"**: It incorporates the informal object pronoun *je* (you). If you are speaking to someone in a formal context, you replace *je* with the formal pronoun *u*.  
• **The particle "wel"**: In Dutch, *wel* is a versatile emphatic particle that roughly translates to "well" or "indeed," adding warmth and emphasis to the gratitude.  
• **Extensions**:  
  – Dankuwel, meneer. (Thank you very much, sir. – *formal*)  
  – Dank je, Martin. (Thanks, Martin. – *slightly shorter and more casual*)  
  – Alsjeblieft, Martin. (Here you go / Please, Martin. – *constructed the same way, literally "if-you-please"*)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dankjewel voor de lekkere koffie, Anna. (Thank you very much for the delicious coffee, Anna.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch culture is notoriously egalitarian and informal. Addressing someone by their first name (Martin) and using the informal *je* (in *dankjewel*) is the standard norm in almost all daily situations, including between bosses and employees, or with service staff. You generally only switch to the formal *dankuwel* for the elderly, high-ranking officials, or in very traditional client-facing businesses.

sentences.nl: Gianluca komt de kamer binnen.
sentences.en: Gianluca comes into the room.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Gianluca = Gianluca  
• komt = comes  
• de = the  
• kamer = room  
• binnen = inside  
• (Natural translation: Gianluca enters the room.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Separable Verb (*Scheidbaar werkwoord*):** The key verb here is *binnenkomen* (to enter / to come inside). In the present tense, the verb splits into two parts. The main verb (*komt*) stays in the second position, while the prefix (*binnen*) gets sent to the very end of the sentence.  
• **No Preposition Needed:** Unlike English ("comes *into* the room"), Dutch uses the direct object (*de kamer*) directly with the separable verb *binnenkomen*, so no extra preposition is needed.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik loop het huis binnen. (I walk into the house.)  
  – De trein rijdt het station binnen. (The train pulls into the station.)  
  – Wanneer kom je binnen? (When are you coming inside?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De docent stapt het klaslokaal binnen. (The teacher steps into the classroom.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• When someone knocks on a door in the Netherlands, the standard way to invite them to enter is simply calling out *"Binnen!"* (short for *Kom binnen* - Come in). Furthermore, when entering a waiting room (like at the doctor's or dentist's) or an elevator, it is a strong Dutch social norm to greet everyone already in the room with a general *"Goedemorgen"* (Good morning) or *"Hallo"*.

sentences.nl: Marieke kijkt op.
sentences.en: Marieke looks up.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke: Marieke  
• kijkt: looks  
• op: up  
*(Natural translation: Marieke looks up.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Separable Verb (*Scheidbaar werkwoord*):** The infinitive verb here is *opkijken* (to look up). In a simple present tense main clause, the verb splits: the conjugated root (*kijkt*) stays in the second position, and the prefix (*op*) moves to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ik sta vroeg **op**. (I get up early. – from *opstaan*)  
  – Hij belt zijn moeder **op**. (He calls up his mother. – from *opbellen*)  
  – Wij kijken **op** van het nieuws. (We are surprised by the news. – idiom using *opkijken van*)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De hond kijkt snel op als ik de kamer binnenkom. (The dog quickly looks up when I enter the room.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• *Marieke* is a very traditional and classic Dutch female name (originally a diminutive of Maria). While *opkijken* literally means "to look up" physically, you will very often hear Dutch people use it with the preposition * tegen* (*opkijken tegen iemand*) to mean admiring or looking up to someone, or *ergens tegenop kijken* which means dreading a difficult task.

kijkt.form_note: 3rd person singular (zij/Marieke) present tense of the separable verb 'opkijken' (stem 'kijk' + t); the prefix 'op' is placed at the end of the sentence
kijkt.fast_speech: Together with 'op', it is pronounced as one word with linking: /kɛi̯kt‿ɔp/

op.form_note: separated prefix of the separable verb 'opkijken', placed at the end of the main clause

sentences.nl: Wauw.
sentences.en: Wow.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wauw. = Wow.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Grammar:** *Wauw* is an interjection (tussenwerpsel) used to express surprise, admiration, or amazement. It stands outside the standard grammatical structure of a sentence. When followed by a full clause, it is separated by a comma, and it does not trigger inversion (the verb does not come immediately after *wauw*).  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Wauw, dat is echt mooi! (Wow, that is really beautiful!)  
  – Wauw, wat een verrassing! (Wow, what a surprise!)  
  – Wauw, heb je dat zelf gemaakt? (Wow, did you make that yourself?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wauw, ik wist niet dat je zo goed Nederlands kon spreken! (Wow, I didn't know you could speak Dutch so well!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While *wauw* is borrowed from English, it is completely integrated into daily Dutch and spelled phonetically according to Dutch rules (using the *au* diphthong). For a more traditionally Dutch equivalent, locals often use *Goh* (expresses mild surprise, like "Gee" or "Gosh") or *Jeetje* (a mild exclamation, similar to "Jeez").

wauw.form_note: Invariable exclamation used to express surprise, admiration, or amazement.

sentences.nl: Voor wie zijn die bloemen?
sentences.en: Who are those flowers for?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Voor (For) wie (who/whom) zijn (are) die (those) bloemen (flowers)?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Preposition Fronting:** Unlike everyday English, where prepositions often go at the end of a question ("Who are those flowers for?"), standard Dutch keeps the preposition (*voor*) together with the question word (*wie*) at the very beginning of the sentence.
• **Inversion:** After the question phrase (*Voor wie*), the verb (*zijn*) must come immediately next, before the subject (*die bloemen*). 
• **Demonstrative Pronoun:** *Die* (those/that) is used here instead of *dat* because *bloemen* is a plural noun (and a *de*-word). All plural nouns take *de* and *die/deze*.
• **Extensions:**
  – Voor wie is dit cadeau? (Who is this gift for?)
  – Met wie ga je naar het feest? (Who are you going to the party with?)
  – Over wie praten jullie? (Who are you guys talking about?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Voor wie heb je deze lekkere taart gebakken? (Who did you bake this delicious cake for?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Flower Culture:** The Netherlands is the flower capital of the world, and giving a *bosje bloemen* (bunch of flowers) is deeply ingrained in Dutch culture. It is the standard gift when invited to someone's home for dinner or a birthday, as well as a common everyday purchase to brighten up one's own living room.

voor.form_note: placed before the question word 'wie' to ask who the recipient is (unlike in English, where 'for' often goes at the end of the sentence)
voor.fast_speech: often shortened to /vɔr/ or /vər/ when unstressed

wie.form_note: question word used for people; object of the preposition 'voor'

zijn.form_note: 3rd person plural present tense of the irregular verb 'zijn' (to be), agreeing with the plural subject 'die bloemen'
zijn.fast_speech: in casual speech often reduced to /zən/ and final -n may be dropped: /zɛi/

die.form_note: plural form (used for 'those' with all plural nouns, regardless of whether the singular is a de-word or het-word)

bloemen.form_note: plural of bloem: regular plural rule, add -en

sentences.nl: Die zijn voor jou.
sentences.en: They're for you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Die – Those / They  
• zijn – are  
• voor – for  
• jou – you  
• *Full translation: Those are for you.*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Die vs. Dat:** *Die* is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "that" (singular, for *de*-words) or "those" (plural, for all nouns). Since the verb here is *zijn* (are), *die* is plural and translates to "those" or "they."  
• **Jij vs. Jou:** *Jou* is the stressed object pronoun for "you" (singular, informal). Because it follows the preposition *voor* (for), you must use the object form *jou* instead of the subject form *jij*. Note that *jouw* with a 'w' means "your" (possessive), though they sound identical.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Dit is voor mij. (This is for me.)  
  – Die bloemen zijn voor haar. (Those flowers are for her.)  
  – Is dat cadeau voor hem? (Is that gift for him?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Deze koekjes zijn speciaal voor jullie. (These cookies are especially for you guys.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using *jou* implies an informal relationship (friends, family, children, or peers). In the Netherlands, people switch to informal pronouns very quickly, even with colleagues or store clerks. However, if you are giving something to an elderly person, a superior, or a client in a formal setting, you would replace *jou* with the formal *u*: "Die zijn voor u."

die.meaning: they / those (pointing back to plural things mentioned earlier)
die.form_note: plural demonstrative pronoun used independently as the subject of the sentence. Dutch often uses 'die' instead of 'zij/ze' (they) to refer back to objects.

zijn.form_note: 3rd person plural present tense of the irregular verb 'zijn' (to be), matching the plural subject 'die'
zijn.fast_speech: in casual speech often pronounced with a schwa: /zən/

voor.form_note: indicates the receiver ('for you'), in contrast to the lesson's grammar point 'van' which indicates the giver of an item, order, or permission
voor.fast_speech: often shortened to /vɔr/ or /vər/ when unstressed

jou.form_note: stressed object form of 'jij', required here because it follows a preposition ('voor') and carries emphasis
jou.fast_speech: if the speaker does not want to emphasize 'you', they replace 'jou' with 'je' (/jə/)

sentences.nl: Marieke fluistert tegen Annika.
sentences.en: Marieke whispers to Annika.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke (Marieke) fluistert (whispers) tegen (to/against) Annika (Annika).  
• Natural translation: Marieke whispers to Annika.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Preposition Use (*tegen*):** Literally meaning "against," the preposition *tegen* is commonly used in Dutch with verbs of speaking (like *praten*, *zeggen*, *schreeuwen*, and *fluisteren*) to mean "to" a person. Note that for whispering specifically, you can also use *in het oor van* (in the ear of) or *naar* (towards).  
• **Verb Conjugation:** The verb is *fluisteren* (to whisper). The stem is *fluister*, and for the third-person singular (she/Marieke) in the present tense, you add a *-t*, making it *fluistert*.  
• **Word Order:** This sentence follows the standard main clause Subject-Verb-Object/Prepositional Phrase (SVO) order.

**Extensions:**  
• Hij praat tegen zijn hond. (He talks to his dog.)  
• Waarom schreeuw je tegen mij? (Why are you yelling at me?)  
• Zij fluistert een geheim. (She whispers a secret.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De leraar zegt iets belangrijks tegen de studenten. (The teacher says something important to the students.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, there is an old-fashioned saying often told to children: *"Fluisteren is liegen"* (Whispering is lying) or *"Wie fluistert, die liegt"* (He who whispers, lies). Because Dutch culture generally values directness and openness, whispering in the presence of others in a social setting is often considered quite rude and exclusionary.

marieke.meaning: Marieke (female first name); the subject of the sentence performing the action.

fluistert.form_note: 3rd person singular (zij/Marieke) present tense of the regular verb fluisteren: stem (fluister) + -t.

tegen.meaning: to (used in Dutch with verbs of speaking like praten, zeggen, and fluisteren to indicate the person being spoken to, whereas English uses 'to').

annika.meaning: Annika (female first name); object of the preposition tegen (the person being whispered to).

sentences.nl: Je mag van mij wel even naar je kamer gaan.
sentences.en: You can go to your room for a bit, if you like.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Je** – You  
• **mag** – may / are allowed to  
• **van mij** – from me (idiomatic: "as far as I'm concerned" / "I give you permission")  
• **wel** – [affirmative/softening particle]  
• **even** – briefly / for a bit  
• **naar je kamer** – to your room  
• **gaan** – to go  

• *Natural translation:* "You are welcome to go to your room for a bit as far as I'm concerned." / "I don't mind if you go to your room for a while."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Mogen van (iemand):** To express who is giving permission in Dutch, the modal verb *mogen* (may/to be allowed to) is paired with the preposition *van* (from). So, *mag van mij* literally means "is allowed from me."
• **Modal Particles (*wel even*):** Combining *wel* and *even* makes the permission sound casual, friendly, and low-pressure. *Wel* reassures the listener ("it's fine"), and *even* minimizes the action ("just for a moment").
• **Word Order (Verb Final):** Because there is a modal verb (*mag*) in the second position, the main action verb (*gaan*) is pushed all the way to the end of the sentence in its infinitive form.

**Extensions:**
• Je **mag van mij** dat laatste koekje opeten. (You can eat that last cookie as far as I'm concerned.)
• Hij **mag van zijn moeder** niet buiten spelen. (His mother won't let him play outside.)
• Je mag hier **wel even** wachten. (You are welcome to wait here for a bit.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Je mag van mij wel even mijn fiets lenen om naar de winkel te gaan. (I don't mind if you borrow my bike for a bit to go to the store.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch communication relies heavily on "verzachters" (softeners)—small filler words like *wel*, *even*, *gewoon*, and *hoor*. Without *wel even*, the sentence (*Je mag van mij naar je kamer gaan*) sounds quite stern and authoritarian, like a parent dismissing a child after an argument. Adding *wel even* transforms it into a gentle, hospitable suggestion (e.g., telling a tired guest they can go rest).

je.form_note: unstressed possessive pronoun, 2nd person singular (stressed form: jouw). Modifies the noun 'kamer'.

mag.form_note: present tense, 2nd person singular (je) of the irregular modal verb 'mogen' (note: no -t added for je/hij with 'mogen'). Combines with the infinitive 'gaan' at the end of the sentence, and pairs with 'van mij' to show who gives the permission.

van.meaning: from / by (indicating the giver of permission)
van.form_note: used here in the construction 'mogen van + person' to indicate who grants the permission ('van mij' = as far as I'm concerned / I allow it).
van.fast_speech: Before 'mij', the /n/ often assimilates to /m/: /vɑm mɛi/

mij.form_note: stressed object pronoun, 1st person singular (unstressed form: me). Object of the preposition 'van'. Stressed here to emphasize that *I* am giving the permission.

wel.meaning: all right / if you like (reassuring tone)
wel.form_note: modal particle used here to soften the permission and make it sound friendly, reassuring, or non-strict.

even.meaning: for a bit / for a moment
even.form_note: indicates a short duration of time, and also makes the sentence sound more casual and friendly.
even.fast_speech: final -n is usually dropped: /ˈeːvə/; in very casual speech often shortened to 'effe' /ˈɛfə/

naar.form_note: preposition of direction indicating movement towards a place ('naar je kamer').
naar.fast_speech: In fast speech, the vowel is often shortened: /nɑr/

kamer.form_note: singular common-gender (de) noun. Plural is formed by adding -s because it ends in an unstressed syllable (-er).

gaan.form_note: infinitive form of the irregular verb 'gaan'; placed at the end of the sentence because it is governed by the modal verb 'mag'.

sentences.nl: Annika laat Marieke en Gianluca alleen.
sentences.en: Annika leaves Marieke and Gianluca alone.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Annika** = Annika  
• **laat** = leaves / lets  
• **Marieke en Gianluca** = Marieke and Gianluca  
• **alleen** = alone  
*(Natural translation: Annika leaves Marieke and Gianluca alone.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Verb-Adjective Collocation (*alleen laten*):** The verb *laten* usually means "to let" or "to allow," but when paired with the adjective *alleen* (alone), it translates to "to leave (someone) alone."  
• **Sentence Bracket (De Tangconstructie):** Notice how the verb *laat* (in the 2nd position) and the adjective *alleen* (at the very end) form a bracket around the direct object (*Marieke en Gianluca*). In Dutch, words that are closely linked to the main verb get pushed to the end of the clause.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Laat mij met rust!* (Leave me in peace! / Leave me alone! — used when annoyed).  
  – *Hij laat zijn hond nooit alleen thuis.* (He never leaves his dog home alone.)  
  – *Kun je ons even alleen laten?* (Can you leave us alone for a moment?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De moeder laat de slapende baby geen seconde alleen. (The mother doesn't leave the sleeping baby alone for a second.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, there is a big social difference between *iemand alleen laten* (used in your sentence) and *iemand met rust laten*. *Alleen laten* literally means physically walking away so people have privacy (like Annika giving Marieke and Gianluca space to talk). If someone is bothering you and you want them to back off, you would say *"Laat me met rust!"* (Leave me in peace), not *"Laat me alleen."*

laat.form_note: 3rd person singular (zij/Annika) present tense of the verb 'laten' (to let / to leave); here used in the fixed combination 'alleen laten' (to leave alone). Because the stem of 'laten' already ends in -t, no extra -t is added.

marieke.form_note: part of the direct object ('Marieke en Gianluca')

en.form_note: coordinating conjunction connecting the two names in the direct object
en.fast_speech: often reduced to /ən/ or /n/ between two words

gianluca.form_note: part of the direct object ('Marieke en Gianluca')

alleen.form_note: uninflected predicative adjective placed at the end of the clause; combines with 'laat' to form the expression 'alleen laten' (to leave someone alone / by themselves)

sentences.nl: Marieke, zegt Gianluca.
sentences.en: Marieke, says Gianluca.
sentences.note: Captions glued this to the next line.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke, → Marieke,  
• zegt → says  
• Gianluca. → Gianluca.  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion in Dialogue Tags:** In Dutch, when a dialogue tag follows a spoken word or quote, the verb comes immediately after the comma, followed by the subject (Verb + Subject). This is called inversion. The spoken part acts as the first element of the sentence, forcing the verb (*zegt*) into the second position.  
• **Verb Conjugation:** *Zegt* is the third-person singular present tense of the verb *zeggen* (to say).  
• **Extensions:**  
– "Hallo," zegt de man. ("Hello," says the man.)  
– "Tot morgen," zegt mijn collega. ("See you tomorrow," says my colleague.)  
– "Ja," zegt zij. ("Yes," she says.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Welkom," zegt de leraar. ("Welcome," says the teacher.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Quotation Marks in Dutch:** In Dutch literature and journalism, it is very common to use single quotation marks ('Marieke,' zegt Gianluca) or no quotation marks at all for dialogue, relying solely on the comma and the "zegt [Name]" structure to show someone is speaking.  
• **Introducing Yourself:** Simply stating your first name while shaking hands (effectively just saying "Marieke" or "Gianluca") is the standard, most natural way to introduce yourself in casual and semi-formal Dutch settings.

marieke.form_note: proper noun; here used to address someone directly (vocative) at the start of a quote

zegt.form_note: 3rd person singular (hij) present tense of zeggen (stem zeg + -t); placed before the subject 'Gianluca' because the spoken quote 'Marieke' is in the first position (inversion)

gianluca.form_note: proper noun; subject of the verb 'zegt'

sentences.nl: Ik vind je erg leuk.
sentences.en: I like you a lot.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ik** – I  
• **vind** – find (consider/like)  
• **je** – you  
• **erg** – very / really  
• **leuk** – nice / likable / fun  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Idiomatic structure (*iemand leuk vinden*):** In English, we use the verb "to like." In Dutch, there is no single verb for this. Instead, the Dutch use the verb *vinden* (to find/have an opinion) combined with the adjective *leuk* (nice/fun). Literally, you are saying "I find you nice."  
• **Word order:** The object (*je*) goes in the middle of the sentence, and the adjective (*leuk*) is pushed toward the end.  
• **Intensifier (*erg*):** Literally meaning "bad" or "severe," *erg* is very commonly used as an adverb meaning "very" or "really" to strengthen an adjective (similar to how English uses "terribly" or "awfully").  
• **Pronoun choice:** *Je* is the unstressed object pronoun for "you." If you wanted to emphasize that you like *this* specific person and no one else, you would use the stressed form: *jou*.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik vind deze film erg leuk. (I really like this movie.)  
• Vind je haar leuk? (Do you like her?)  
• Hij vindt zijn nieuwe baan erg leuk. (He really likes his new job.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik vind het erg leuk om met jou te praten. (I really like talking with you.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Romantic vs. Platonic:** In Dutch dating culture, saying *Ik vind je leuk* or *Ik vind je erg leuk* is the standard way to confess romantic feelings or tell someone you have a crush on them,long before the heavy *Ik hou van je* (I love you) is used. While you can use it platonically for friends, saying it one-on-one with a serious tone will almost always be interpreted as romantic interest.

ik.fast_speech: often reduced to /k/ in fast speech before a verb: /k ˈfɪnt/

vind.form_note: 1st person singular (ik) present tense of vinden; stem without -t, final d is pronounced /t/
vind.fast_speech: before 'je', final /t/ + /j/ often merges into /tʃ/: 'vind je' sounds like /ˈvɪntʃə/

je.form_note: 2nd person singular unstressed object pronoun (the stressed form is 'jou')

erg.form_note: used as an adverb here to intensify the adjective 'leuk'
erg.fast_speech: a schwa is often inserted between /r/ and /x/, making it sound like 'erreg': /ˈɛrəx/

leuk.form_note: predicative adjective describing the object 'je', so it takes no -e ending

sentences.nl: Ik wil dat je dat weet.
sentences.en: I want you to know that.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) wil (want) dat (that) je (you) dat (that) weet (know).  
• Natural translation: I want you to know that.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Expressing "want [someone] to [do]":** Unlike English, which uses an object + infinitive ("want you to know"), Dutch uses the conjunction *dat* (that) to introduce a subordinate clause ("want that you know").  
• **Subordinate clause word order:** Because *dat* introduces a subordinate clause (bijzin), the conjugated verb *weet* is pushed to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Double "dat":** The first *dat* is a conjunction ("that"), and the second *dat* is a demonstrative pronoun ("that [thing/fact]").  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik wil dat je naar huis komt. (I want you to come home.)  
• Hij wil dat we dat doen. (He wants us to do that.)  
• Ik hoop dat je dat begrijpt. (I hope that you understand that.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik wil dat je mij morgen belt. (I want you to call me tomorrow.)

ik.fast_speech: in unstressed position before a consonant, sometimes reduced to /k/

wil.form_note: 1st person singular (ik) present tense of the irregular modal verb 'willen'

dat.meaning: that (direct object of 'weet', referring to a piece of information)
dat.form_note: demonstrative pronoun (neuter singular), used independently here as a direct object

je.form_note: 2nd person singular unstressed subject pronoun (stressed form: jij)
je.fast_speech: after 'dat', often merges with /t/ to sound like /tʃə/

weet.form_note: 2nd person singular (je) present tense of the strong/irregular verb 'weten'; placed at the end because of the conjunction 'dat' (stem 'weet' already ends in -t, so no extra -t is added)

sentences.nl: Daarom heb ik bloemen voor je gekocht.
sentences.en: That's why I bought you flowers.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Daarom (Therefore / That's why) + heb (have) + ik (I) + bloemen (flowers) + voor (for) + je (you) + gekocht (bought).  
• Natural English: "That's why I bought flowers for you."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion after "Daarom":** *Daarom* is a conjunctive adverb. When a sentence starts with it, the subject and the finite verb swap places so the verb stays in the second position (*Daarom **heb ik**...* instead of *Daarom ik heb...*).  
• **Present Perfect (Voltooid Tegenwoordige Tijd):** Dutch uses the present perfect to describe completed past actions where English often uses the simple past. It is formed here with the auxiliary verb *hebben* (conjugated as *heb*) + the past participle *gekocht* (from the irregular verb *kopen* - to buy).  
• **Verb Placement:** In the present perfect, the conjugated auxiliary verb (*heb*) takes the second position, while the past participle (*gekocht*) goes all the way to the end of the clause.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Daarom ben ik vandaag thuis gebleven.* (That's why I stayed home today.)  
  – *Ik heb een cadeautje voor je gekocht.* (I bought a little gift for you.)  
  – *Daarom heb ik het niet gedaan.* (That's why I didn't do it.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Daarom heb ik een lekkere taart voor je gebakken. (That's why I baked a delicious cake for you.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Netherlands is the global heart of the floral industry, making flowers a very common, affordable, and appreciated gift for almost any occasion (birthdays, dinner invitations, or apologies). When bringing flowers to a Dutch home, it is customary to remove the store's price tag, though you leave the paper wrapping on when handing them over to the host.

daarom.form_note: pronominal adverb at the start of the sentence; triggers inversion so the verb 'heb' comes before the subject 'ik'

heb.meaning: have (auxiliary verb for the present perfect)
heb.form_note: 1st person singular (ik) present tense of hebben, used as an auxiliary verb with 'gekocht' to form the present perfect tense; placed before 'ik' due to inversion after 'daarom'
heb.fast_speech: Together with 'ik', often pronounced as one unit: /ˈɦɛbɪk/ (final /p/ voices back to /b/ before a vowel)

ik.form_note: 1st person singular subject pronoun; placed after the finite verb 'heb' because the sentence starts with 'daarom'
ik.fast_speech: Often reduced to /ək/ in unstressed position

bloemen.form_note: plural of bloem: add -en; direct object of the sentence

voor.fast_speech: Often shortened to /vɔr/ or /vər/ in quick speech

je.form_note: unstressed 2nd person singular object pronoun after the preposition 'voor'

gekocht.form_note: irregular past participle of kopen; placed at the end of the clause to complete the present perfect tense with 'heb'

sentences.nl: Marieke fleurt een beetje op en natuurlijk moet ze weer blozen.
sentences.en: Marieke cheers up a little, and of course she has to blush again.
sentences.note: opfleuren = cheer up. Captions heard flirt; listen at ~2:40.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke: Marieke
• fleurt: brightens / cheers (from *opfleuren*)
• een beetje: a bit / a little
• op: up (separable prefix of *opfleuren*)
• en: and
• natuurlijk: naturally / of course
• moet: must / has to
• ze: she
• weer: again
• blozen: to blush

(Natural translation: "Marieke perks up a bit and of course, she blushes again.")

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Separable Verb (*opfleuren*):** The verb *opfleuren* (to cheer up/brighten up) is separable. In a main clause, the stem (*fleurt*) stays in the second position, and the prefix (*op*) is pushed to the end of that clause. 
• **Inversion after *natuurlijk*:** In the second clause, the adverb *natuurlijk* is placed at the beginning (right after the conjunction *en*). Because the conjugated verb must always be in the second position of a main clause, the verb (*moet*) and the subject (*ze*) swap places: *natuurlijk moet ze* instead of *natuurlijk ze moet*.
• **Idiomatic *moeten*:** Using *moeten* (must/have to) with involuntary emotional or physical reactions (like *blozen*, *lachen*, *huilen*) is very common in Dutch. It means you "can't help but" do it, or it "makes you" do it.

**Extensions:**
• De woonkamer **fleurt** echt **op** met die nieuwe planten. (The living room really brightens up with those new plants.)
• **Natuurlijk moet ik** altijd lachen om zijn domme grappen. (Of course, his silly jokes always make me laugh / I always have to laugh at his silly jokes.)
• Ze **moest** een beetje **huilen** bij het einde van de film. (She teared up a bit / couldn't help crying a bit at the end of the movie.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Na het goede nieuws fleurt Tom meteen op en natuurlijk moet hij even glimlachen. (After the good news, Tom immediately perks up and of course, he can't help but smile for a moment.)

sentences.nl: Dat hoefde je toch niet te doen.
sentences.en: You really didn't have to do that.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Dat** (That) **hoefde** (needed [past]) **je** (you) **toch** (really / after all) **niet** (not) **te** (to) **doen** (do).  
• Natural translation: "You really didn't have to do that."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Hoeven + te + infinitive**: The verb *hoeven* (to need to / to have to) is almost exclusively used in negative contexts (with *niet* or *geen*) or with restrictive words like *alleen maar* (only). Unlike standard modal verbs (like *kunnen* or *moeten*), *hoeven* requires the word **te** before the main verb at the end of the sentence (*te doen*).  
• **Inversion**: By placing the object *Dat* at the very beginning of the sentence for emphasis, the subject (*je*) and the conjugated verb (*hoefde*) must swap places (Verb-Second rule).  
• **Modal particle "toch"**: Here, *toch* softens the statement and adds a tone of warmth, reassurance, or mild surprise, similar to adding "really" in English ("You *really* didn't have to...").  
• **Extensions**:  
  – Je hoeft niet te wachten. (You don't have to wait.)  
  – Dat hoef je mij niet te vertellen! (You don't need to tell me that!)  
  – Zij hoefde gisteren niet te werken. (She didn't have to work yesterday.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Die dure wijn hoefde je toch niet te kopen! (You really didn't need to buy that expensive wine!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• This is the standard, polite Dutch response when someone gives you an unexpected gift, pays for your drink, or goes out of their way to do you a favor. Just like "You shouldn't have!" in English, it expresses gratitude through polite modesty rather than actual disapproval.

sentences.nl: Ik weet toch dat je mij leuk vindt.
sentences.en: I know you like me, don't I?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ik (I) weet (know) toch (after all / anyway) dat (that) je (you) mij (me) leuk (nice / likeable) vindt (find).  
• Natural translation: "I know that you like me, don't I?" or "Come on, I know you like me."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **The modal particle "toch":** This is a classic Dutch flavor word with no direct English translation. Here, it expresses certainty, a reminder of an obvious fact, or a teasing appeal for confirmation (similar to "after all," "obviously," or "don't I?").  
• **Subordinate clause word order:** The conjunction *dat* (that) kicks the conjugated verb (*vindt*) to the very end of the sentence: *...dat je mij leuk **vindt**.*  
• **Idiom "leuk vinden":** Dutch doesn't have a single verb for "to like." Instead, they use *leuk vinden* (literally: to find nice).  
• Extensions:  
  – Ik zie toch dat je moe bent. (I can clearly see that you are tired / I see you're tired, don't I?)  
  – Hij weet dat ik haar leuk vind. (He knows that I like her.)  
  – Jij vindt deze film toch ook leuk? (You like this movie too, right?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Jij weet toch dat hij morgen niet kan komen? (You do know that he can't come tomorrow, right?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Dating and "Leuk vinden":** In Dutch dating culture, saying *Ik vind je leuk* (I like you) is the standard way to confess romantic feelings early on. The phrase *Ik hou van je* (I love you) is considered very heavy and is strictly reserved for serious, established relationships.

sentences.nl: Marieke vindt het leuk dat ze bloemen krijgt.
sentences.en: Marieke likes getting flowers.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke: Marieke  
• vindt: finds (thinks/considers)  
• het: it  
• leuk: nice / fun / pleasant  
• dat: that  
• ze: she  
• bloemen: flowers  
• krijgt: gets / receives  

• *Natural translation:* Marieke likes getting flowers / Marieke is happy that she is getting flowers.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Iets leuk vinden (To like something):** Instead of a direct verb like "to like," Dutch often uses *vinden* (to find) + an adjective (like *leuk*). Literally, "to find something nice."  
• **Temporary object 'het':** When the thing you like is an entire clause (starting with *dat*), Dutch requires the placeholder word *het* (it) in the main clause: *vindt **het** leuk dat...*  
• **Subordinate clause word order (Bijzin):** The word *dat* introduces a subordinate clause, which pushes the conjugated verb (*krijgt*) to the very end of the sentence.  

• **Extensions:**  
– Ik vind het jammer dat hij niet komt. (I think it's a pity that he isn't coming.)  
– Wij vinden het fijn dat je helpt. (We like it / are glad that you are helping.)  
– Vind je het goed dat ik het raam openmaak? (Are you okay with it if I open the window?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Thomas vindt het spannend dat hij morgen een nieuwe baan begint. (Thomas finds it exciting that he is starting a new job tomorrow.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Netherlands is the heart of the global flower trade. Because fresh flowers are sold everywhere—from street markets to supermarkets—and are relatively inexpensive, it is a very common custom to bring a bouquet when visiting someone's home for a birthday, dinner, or *op de koffie* (for a coffee visit).

sentences.nl: Gianluca is niet helemaal haar type.

• Gianluca = Gianluca  
• is = is

• haar = her  
• type = type  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Niet helemaal (Partial Negation):** Combining *niet* (not) with *helemaal* (completely/totally) creates a polite softener meaning "not quite" or "not completely." Be careful with word order: *niet helemaal* means "not quite," whereas *helemaal niet* means "not at all."  
• **Noun Gender & Possessives:** Even though *het type* is a neuter noun (het-word), the possessive pronoun *haar* (her) does not change form based on the gender of the noun it modifies.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Dat is niet helemaal waar. (That is not entirely true.)  
  – Ik ben nog niet helemaal klaar. (I am not quite ready yet.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• While the Dutch are famous for being direct, they frequently use *understatement* (like "niet helemaal" or "niet echt") in social situations to soften rejections or negative opinions, so they don't sound unnecessarily harsh.

sentences.nl: Ze vindt Martin eigenlijk leuker.
sentences.en: She actually likes Martin better.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ze – She  
• vindt – finds (thinks/considers)  
• Martin – Martin  
• eigenlijk – actually / in fact  
• leuker – nicer / more likeable  

*(Natural translation: She actually likes Martin better / more.)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Vinden + [object] + [adjective]:** In Dutch, to express an opinion or state whether you like someone/something, you use the verb *vinden* (to find) paired with an adjective. "To like" is literally "to find nice" (*leuk vinden*).  
• **Comparatives:** Adding *-er* to the adjective *leuk* (nice/fun) creates the comparative *leuker* (nicer/more fun). Combined with *vinden*, *leuker vinden* translates to "to like better" or "to prefer."  
• **Word Order with Adverbs:** The adverb *eigenlijk* (actually) is placed after the direct object (*Martin*) and right before the adjective (*leuker*) it modifies.  

**Extensions:**  
• Ik vind koffie eigenlijk lekkerder. (I actually like coffee better [for taste].)  
• Hij vindt deze film spannender. (He finds this movie more exciting.)  
• Vind je haar echt aardig? (Do you really think she is nice / like her?)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wij vinden het oude huis eigenlijk mooier. (We actually like the old house better / find the old house prettier.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch dating and youth culture, saying you find someone *leuk* (*Ik vind hem/haar leuk*) is the standard, everyday way to say you have a crush on them or are romantically interested in them, without the heavy weight of saying "I love you" (*Ik hou van je*). Therefore, *Ze vindt Martin eigenlijk leuker* can easily imply she prefers Martin romantically over someone else.

sentences.nl: Maar ja, die heeft al een vriendin.
sentences.en: But well, he already has a girlfriend.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Maar ja, = But yes, (Well / Oh well,)  
• die = that one (he/she)  
• heeft = has  
• al = already  
• een vriendin. = a girlfriend.  
• (Natural translation: "Oh well, he/she already has a girlfriend.")

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Maar ja**: Literally "but yes," this is a very common conversational filler used to express resignation, acceptance, or moving on from a topic (like "Oh well," "Anyway," or "Then again"). Because it acts as an interjection, it doesn't cause inversion (the verb doesn't immediately follow it).  
• **Die as a personal pronoun**: In spoken Dutch, the demonstrative pronoun *die* ("that/those")very frequently replaces third-person pronouns like *hij* (he), *zij* (she), or *zij* (they) when referring to someone just mentioned.  
• **Al**: A short time adverb meaning "already." Notice how it naturally sits right after the conjugated verb (*heeft*).  

• Extensions:  
– **Maar ja**, wat doe je eraan? (Oh well, what can you do about it?)  
– Waar is Jan? **Die** is **al** naar huis. (Where is Jan? He has already gone home.)  
– Zij **heeft al** een nieuwe baan. (She already has a new job.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik vind dat huis prachtig, maar ja, die is al verkocht.  
(I think that house is gorgeous, oh well, it has already been sold.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Vriendin vs. een vriendin**: In Dutch, *vriendin* means both "female friend" and "girlfriend" (romantic). Context usually clarifies it. Saying *een vriendin van mij* means "a (platonic) female friend of mine," whereas saying someone *heeft een vriendin* (like in your sentence) or talking about *mijn vriendin* almost always implies a romantic partner.

sentences.nl: Kom je even bij me zitten?
sentences.en: Will you come and sit with me for a bit?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Kom (Come) je (you) even (briefly / for a moment) bij (by / next to) me (me) zitten (to sit)?  
• Natural translation: Will you come sit with me for a bit?

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Question Word Order (Inversion):** Because this is a yes/no question, the conjugated verb (*Kom*) is placed before the subject (*je*). Note that the verb drops its *-t* ending when *je/jij* follows it directly (it is *Kom je*, not *Komt je*).  
• **Double Verb Construction:** *Komen* (to come) acts as a helper verb here, pushing the main action verb (*zitten*) in its infinitive form to the very end of the sentence.  
• **Modal Particle *Even*:** Literally meaning "briefly," the word *even* is used here as a softener. It makes the request sound casual, friendly, and low-pressure, much like adding "for a sec" or "just" in English.  
• **Preposition *Bij*:** In this context, *bij* indicates proximity and companionship ("next to" or "with").  
• Extensions:  
– Kom je vanavond bij ons eten? (Are you coming to eat with us tonight?)  
– Mag ik hier even zitten? (May I sit here for a moment?)  
– Hij komt naast me staan. (He comes to stand next to me.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Kom je straks nog even bij ons langs voor een kopje koffie? (Will you drop by our place for a quick cup of coffee later?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using *even* (often shortened to *effe* in spoken Dutch) is essential for sounding natural and polite in the Netherlands. Because the Dutch communication style is quite direct, they rely heavily on softening words like *even* to turn what would otherwise be a blunt command into a warm, *gezellig* (cozy/friendly) invitation.

sentences.nl: Oeh, mag dat van jou?
sentences.en: Ooh, is that okay with you?
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oeh – Ooh  
• mag – may / is allowed  
• dat – that  
• van – from / by  
• jou – you  

*(Natural translation: Ooh, do you allow that? / Ooh, are you okay with that?)*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Mogen van + [person]**: In English, you say "*You* allow that." In Dutch, the thing being allowed becomes the subject (*dat*), and the person giving permission is introduced with the preposition *van* (from/by). Literally, it means "Is that allowed from you?"  
• **Mag (Mogen)**: *Mag* is the singular present tense of the modal verb *mogen* (to be allowed to / may). In Dutch, modal verbs often drop the main action verb (like *doen* - to do) if the context is obvious.  
• **Jou vs. Je**: The stressed form *jou* is used here instead of the unstressed *je* to emphasize the specific person giving the permission ("Are *you* okay with that?").  

• **Extensions:**  
– Dat mag niet van mijn moeder. (My mother doesn't allow that.)  
– Mag ik een koekje van jou? (Can I have a cookie from you / Do you allow me to have a cookie?)  
– Van mij mag je gaan. (As far as I'm concerned, you may go / I allow you to go.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mag de hond van jou op de bank slapen? (Do you allow the dog to sleep on the couch?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Starting a sentence with "Oeh" gives it a playful, teasing, or slightly conspiratorial tone. The Dutch often use this exact phrase when someone is bending a minor rule (like eating a piece of cake before dinner or leaving work five minutes early) to playfully check if the other person is going to "let it slide."

sentences.nl: Ondertussen kijkt Xing stiekem naar Gianluca en Marieke vanuit haar slaapkamer.
sentences.en: Meanwhile Xing secretly watches Gianluca and Marieke from her bedroom.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• **Ondertussen** – Meanwhile  
• **kijkt** – looks / watches  
• **Xing** – Xing  
• **stiekem** – secretly / sneaky  
• **naar** – at  
• **Gianluca en Marieke** – Gianluca and Marieke  
• **vanuit** – from (out of)  
• **haar slaapkamer** – her bedroom  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Inversion (Word Order):** The sentence starts with the time adverb *Ondertussen* (Meanwhile) rather than the subject. Because Dutch requires the verb to be in the second position (V2 rule), the verb (*kijkt*) comes immediately after the adverb, and the subject (*Xing*) moves to the third position.  
• **Fixed Preposition:** The verb *kijken* (to look/watch) pairs with the preposition *naar* to mean "to look at."  
• **Preposition *Vanuit*:** While *van* means "from," *vanuit* specifically means "from the inside of" an enclosed space (like a room, a window, or a car) looking or moving outward.  
• **Extensions:**  
  – *Ondertussen wacht ik op de trein.* (Meanwhile, I wait for the train.)  
  – *Hij luistert stiekem naar hun gesprek.* (He secretly listens to their conversation.)  
  – *Ik werk vandaag vanuit huis.* (I am working from home today.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ondertussen luistert de hond stiekem naar de vogels vanuit de woonkamer. (Meanwhile, the dog secretly listens to the birds from the living room.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The word *stiekem* is a cultural favorite in the Netherlands. While it translates to "secretly" or "on the sly," it often carries a lighthearted, cheeky, or slightly mischievous nuance rather than a sinister one (e.g., *stiekem een koekje pakken* – sneaking a cookie). It is also very commonly used as a filler word to mean "actually" or "deep down" (e.g., *Ik vind het stiekem best leuk* – I actually kind of like it).

sentences.nl: Hm, die Gianluca toch.
sentences.en: Hm, that Gianluca, honestly.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Hm = Hmm  
• die = that  
• Gianluca = Gianluca  
• toch = (modal particle: really / what can you do / after all)  
• *Natural translation: "Hmm, oh that Gianluca."*

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **"Die" + [Name]:** Placing the demonstrative pronoun *die* (that) before a person's name is a very common informal way to refer to someone known to both the speaker and the listener. It often carries an emotional undertone, such as fondness, mild exasperation, or amusement.  
• **The modal particle "toch":** At the end of a verbless phrase like this, *toch* doesn't have a direct translation. Instead, it adds a tone of resignation, shaking your head at someone's typical behavior (like saying "Typical Gianluca!" or "Oh, that Gianluca, what is he like?").  
• **Extensions:**  
  – Ach, die kinderen toch. (Oh, those kids [with a sigh of fondness or exasperation].)  
  – Die Peter weet altijd alles beter. (That Peter always knows better.)  
  – O, die kat van jou toch! (Oh, that cat of yours!)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ha, die oma toch, ze heeft alweer drie taarten gebakken. (Ha, oh that grandma, she baked three pies again.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Using modal particles like *toch*, *hoor*, *hè*, and *even* is the secret to sounding truly Dutch. A phrase like *"Die [Name] toch"* is a classic conversational response when someone tells a story about a mutual friend doing something completely in character (usually something slightly silly, stubborn, or cheeky). It shows empathy and shared understanding without needing a full sentence.

sentences.nl: Wat doet hij dat romantisch.
sentences.en: How romantically he does that.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wat = What / How  
• doet = does  
• hij = he  
• dat = that  
• romantisch = romantically  

(Natural translation: How romantically he does that!)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• **Exclamative "Wat"**: In Dutch, *wat* is frequently used at the beginning of a sentence to make an exclamation (meaning "how" or "what a").  
• **Word Order (V2 Inversion)**: Notice that even though *wat* + *romantisch* go together in meaning ("how romantically"), Dutch separates them. The verb (*doet*) must stay in the second position, followed immediately by the subject (*hij*) and object (*dat*), pushing the adverb (*romantisch*) to the very end.  
• **Adjective as Adverb**: In Dutch, adjectives and adverbs look identical. *Romantisch* means both "romantic" and "romantically."  

**Extensions:**  
• Wat zingt zij dat mooi! (How beautifully she sings that!)  
• Wat zeg je dat lief. (How sweetly you say that.)  
• Wat kookt hij goed! (How well he cooks!)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wat lost ze dat slim op! (How cleverly she solves that!)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• **Sarcasm alert**: Depending on the tone of voice, Dutch speakers very often use this exact *Wat... dat...* structure sarcastically. Since Dutch culture generally favors practicality and directness over grand romantic gestures ("doe maar normaal" – just act normal), saying *"Wat doet hij dat romantisch"* in a flat tone is a very common way to poke fun at someone being overly cheesy or failing at being romantic.
